questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: ETH Zürich is a very good educational and research institution with very interesting and advanced courses in biology, which is a big reason for why I chose ETH. Moreover, I wanted to explore Switzerland because of the amazing nature of course and the high quality of life

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Easy, you will generally get emails about everything you need to know and do

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The exchange office of ETH were very helpful and provided all necessary information by email. They also held some intro events that were helpful.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I was offered a room at a student housing for exchange students through WOKO, which is the student housing cooperation of Zurich, and they have many rooms that you can apply for. It is not guaranteed to get a room though, and you have to be quick once the application form opens (for me it was around may). It might take a little more time to find housing if you dont get it through woko, but there are other student houses you can apply for, although you might have to be a bit early. Renting of rooms/apartments (not student housing) is generally expensive

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Most places are well-connected to campus through public transport, which is quite reliable, so it is also fine to live a bit outside of the city center/outside of Zürich. I would highly recommend applying for the WOKO rooms or other student houses, as it is very enriching to live with other (exchange) students, when you dont have any other network when you arrive.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It was quite straight forward, you just fill out an application and if you have already been granted an exchange spot from UCPH, this should not cause problems.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: It was easy to find answers to most questions you could have on the ETH website. The exchange coordinators from ETH were also very helpful and quick to reply to emails

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
I took one course that had limited amount of spots, so I was put on a waiting list because I, as an exchange student, had the lowest priority for receiving a spot. In the end, there were available spots though. Most "normal" courses (in D-BIOL) dont have a maximum capacity, and you can register/deregister as you wish. I also took a seminar course with only 15 spots, where masters students had priority, so I had to wait until a registration deadline to know if I received a spot, which I did.
I took 3 block courses, which are special to D-BIOL. For these, you dont register through the normal registration portal, but through a specific website. The registration opening date is a bit later than normal registration, and you make a priority list of which block courses you want to attend. A few weeks later, you are told for which ones you have been given a spot. In the first block, I did not get my first priority, but my third or fourth (I ended up loving this course though). The other block courses were my first priority

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Keep your email notifications on, so that you know when the registration opens, if you want to register for any courses with a limited capacity. It is generally on a first come first serve basis. If there is no mention of a maximum capacity in the course catalogue, then you can register for the course whenever you want (even in the middle of the semester)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The level and workload is generally quite high, and I felt much more busy with my studies at ETH than I do at UCPH. My impression is that most of the other exchange students felt the same. It was, however, also extremely interesting and I learned a lot.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took mostly bachelor's level courses, but I took one masters' seminar course. The level was high in all the courses, but I definitely did not feel like I lagged behind as a student from UCPH compared to the ETH students.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: A lot of courses were lecture-only courses, where there were no problem-solving classes or something similar. I did not like this, as it was less motivating and harder to retain the knowledge from the lectures. The block courses, however, were amazing and I would highly recommend taking as many as possible if you are enrolled in D-BIOL. These were much smaller classes, where you got to know your teachers more personally and got a lot of hands-on experience and were exposed to the actual research the teachers are doing, which was super fun. It was much more collaborative and similar to classes in gymnasium, so you got to know the other (swiss) students as well

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Systems Biology of Metabolism (MA)
Immunology I (BA)
Molecular Structure and Function: Proteins (BA)
Introduction to Mass Spectrometry-Based Proteomics (BA)
Insulin Signaling (BA)
Parallels Between Tissue Repair and Cancer (BA)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Immunology and Molecular Structure and Function were both quite interesting, but they were each only one lecture per week, so I didnt find it very engaging or motivating. I personally like immunology better, and it follows up quite nicely from Medical Cell and Tissue Biology (if you are a biomedicine student)
Systems Biology of Metabolism was a super interesting seminar course, where you had to read 1-3 papers each week and discuss them in class. The two professors are super nice and talented. I did not have the right prerequisites in Systems Biology though, so I definitely felt that it was hard to follow along al lot of the time. It ended up going well in the end though, so dont be scared if you think the topic sounds interesting. I learned a lot.
Introduction to Mass Spectrometry Based Proteomics and Insulin Signaling were both amazing block courses. The teachers were very nice and very good, and the content was super interesting. I learned a lot from both of them, that I could also use in my other courses. Would 10/10 recommend
Parallels Between Tissue Repair and Cancer was also a block course, but it was far less organized than the two others, so the overall experience was not that good. The content was interesting though, but I think I could have learned more from other courses. We did get to work with organoids which was very fun, and you get good insight into what its like to work as a PhD or postdoc in a research group

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Public transport, in particular transport outside the city, is VERY expensive. I usually went on a trip to go hiking/skiing/sightseeing every weekend, so this became very expensive

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Everything is expensive, even coming from Denmark. Coffee is a little cheaper than in Denmark. I did not have to buy any textbooks, so this was cheaper than expected

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
As a student, you can become a member (for free!) at ASVZ, which is the student sports association. This gives you free access to gyms and a lot of different sports classes
There were also big parties for the entire school a few times during the semester. I would recommend to check out the PolyBall, which is a big traditional ball. The main building is very nicely decorated and it is cool to attend. You can take ball-dancing crash courses in advance, which I did (learnt english waltz, discofox, jive and more)
ESN Zurich also have many events for exchange students throughout the semester

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go see the nature of Switzerland as early as possible, before it becomes too cold and snowy to go hiking (usually around november). There are so many incredible places to go.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: The alps. Both for hiking and for skiing

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy, not too dissimilar from the danish

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I only socialized with local students because of the block courses I took, so if you have the opportunity to do this, I would recommend it.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: It is quite orderly, so people generally follow rules, which means that e.g. you very rarely get your ticket checked on busses/trams, self-checkout at the supermarket is very smooth and you dont have to scan your receipt, cars ALWAYS stop for you immediately if you want to cross the road etc. Public transport is also generally on time and very reliable. It is also very clean everywhere

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Do stuff with other exchange students when you get the opportunity, especially in the beginning. Dont be afraid to be the one to reach out and take initiative, often other people will also not know who to talk to/do stuff with, so people are very open and friendly. 
It is fun to get to know some of the local swiss students, but realistically, you are probably gonna get to know other exchange students better. They are in the same boat as you, and also dont know anyone and want to experience as much as possible. The swiss students already have an established network and can be harder to get to know, because they are less interested in doing stuff e.g. on the weekends.
Study in the weekdays and do fun stuff on the weekends, such as daytrips to other places or anything else that sounds fun.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
You can get a "friends daypass for youth", which is a public transport daypass for 4 people under 25, that you can use for a whole day to take any public transport in Switzerland. Only costs 80francs, definitely the cheapest way to get around outside of Zurich
You can also buy a half-fare pass, which means you get 50% off all public transport tickets you buy. If you plan to take public transport everyday to campus and live in zone 110, you can get a monthly 110 pass for 60francs, which is cheaper than buying a ticket everyday, even with the half-fare
You can register for a 2-week intensive german course, that lies in the two weeks before the semester start. This is a great way to make friends in the very beginning, if you want to learn some basic german or freshen up your high-school german. You can also use the first two weeks of september to explore switzerland before the courses begin in mid-september

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friends I made and the academic things I learned

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Some of the courses were harder than I was used to, and I felt unsure of whether I would manage, however it worked out in the end

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
